generalizedRange: Atlantic Forest of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
hook: A third of the wild ones descend from zoo-born monkeys. It worked.

story.text: The golden lion tamarin is a monkey small enough to hold, crowned with a backswept golden mane like a miniature lion's.
Families of two to eight sleep from dusk to sunrise in tree holes, tucked together for warmth.
Mothers usually bear twins — rare among primates — and the adult male does the largest share of the carrying.
Its Atlantic Forest home has been cut to two percent of its original area, scattered into islands of green.
By the 1960s, fewer than two hundred remained.
So zoos rebuilt the species: between 1984 and 2001, 146 tamarins born in 43 institutions on three continents went home to Brazil.
It worked. About a third of wild golden lion tamarins today descend from animals raised in human care.
The forest is being resewn too: restored pastures, corridor plantings, and a forested overpass that carries tamarins across a highway.
When yellow fever killed a third of the species, conservationists answered by vaccinating wild monkeys — over five hundred so far.
To witness the golden lion tamarin is to see what patience across generations can rebuild: roughly 4,800 now leap through the canopy.

reproduction.text: Twins are the rule, born fully furred with eyes open. The whole family raises them, the adult male carrying most of all. Females mature at eighteen months, males at two years.

insight.text: The 146-tamarin reintroduction, drawing on 43 institutions in eight countries, has been called perhaps the most collaborative conservation effort in history.

programs.title: Grow Trees for GLTs
programs.summary: Local farmers grow native seedlings that are planted as forest corridors reconnecting the fragments tamarins live in.
